synopsis: UNECE’s VMAD-developed NATM treats simulation as one evidence pillar alongside track testing, real-world testing and audit; physical tests remain the default, virtual results are spot-checked, and the number of R152 physical confirmation tests is left to manufacturer–authority agreement [f1281, f1282, f1284, f172]. Its credibility framework defines the envelope of permitted virtual-tool use and covers accuracy, robustness, documentation, verification and validation, calibration, sensitivity analysis, management and team expertise [f6929, f4830, f7143]. A January 2024 working-group paper nevertheless found that the R152 virtual-testing proposal did not yet address every aspect of a credible capability [f1218]. The corpus identifies 2022 NATM guidelines and a March 2023 master document, while another chapter attributes the master document to 2022, leaving a document-date ambiguity [f7143, f8101, f6929]. UNECE and ISO scenario methods can help establish representative virtual-test coverage, but no direct equivalent of UNECE toolchain credibility principles was found for automatic braking on earth-moving machines, so these on-road precedents do not establish an off-road-specific framework [f8031, f7740, f4831].
